lines.note: Continues the preceding page’s proverb: the great elephant does not play on the hare’s narrow path. The Japanese aſobazu is the negative of asobu; the line begins in mid-example.

runs.text: brinca no caminho eſtreito da lebrè. i, Cada hũ

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the elephant-and-hare contrast, then introduces its interpretation with i, Cada hũ, meaning each individual. The grave accent on lebrè is retained as printed.

runs.text: tem ſeu lugar de recreação conueniente.

lines.note: Completes the proverb’s interpretation: everyone has a suitable place for recreation. This is the end of the preceding entry, not part of the following clock definition.
Tokei means a clock; suna no tokei is a sand clock. The Portuguese Re- begins relogio across the physical line break.
Logio completes relogio darea, a clock of sand. The historical joined darea is preserved rather than expanded.
Tooken is explained by katana and ken, matching the Portuguese pair of sword names. The scan shows q, correcting the OCR Tǒjen; the caron remains distinct from a circumflex.
Tooken mujun gathers sword, spear and shield vocabulary under offensive arms. Offenſiuas has no extra i after u; the printed gloss is preserved even though the Japanese combination includes shields.
This separate tooken is kara no inu, a dog from China. The joined Cãoda is retained from the print rather than regularized to modern Portuguese spacing.
Token names the bird called hototogisu. The initial is a capital T, not the OCR r; Fototoguiſu is a Japanese bird name embedded in a Portuguese explanation.
Toketsu is explained as chi wo haku yamai, an illness involving vomiting blood. The final bare t is the historical checked coda, not a missing printed syllable.
Completes lançarſangue polla boca, bringing blood out through the mouth. The close printed spacing and historical polla are retained.
Toki is time or an hour. Toki wo hakaru means measuring time, and the Portuguese Me- continues into medir on the next row.

runs.text: dir o tempo, ou as horas. ¶

lines.note: Completes measuring time or the hours, then begins toki wo matsu, waiting for the proper time. The Japanese verb is divided at the physical row boundary.
Tçu completes matsu. The gloss is waiting for a time or opportunity; the next example begins To- and continues below.
Completes toki wo ushinoo, losing time or an opportunity. Preserve the caron in vxinǒ and the historical initial v rather than substituting modern romanization.
Toki wo toru and tokidori wo suru introduce choosing a time; Latin l gives the alternative. To- begins the Portuguese infinitive tomar on the following line.

runs.text: mar, ou escolher tẽpo por agouro pera fazer al-

lines.note: The chosen time is selected by divination before an undertaking. The abbreviated tẽpo remains unexpanded, and al- continues into algũa.
Completes doing something at the chosen time, then gives toki ga utsuru, the passing or changing of time. The punctuation after Mudarſe is a comma in the scan.

runs.text: ou paßarſe o tempo, & as horas. ¶

lines.note: Completes the gloss about time and hours passing; toki starts the next example and links to itaru below.

runs.text: Chegarſe, ou vir a hora determinada

lines.note: Toki itaru means that the appointed hour arrives. The Portuguese reads vir a hora, with a visible separation between the infinitive and article.
Hanjoo no toki itatta illustrates the arrival of a time of flourishing; the next line specifies propagation of the religious law. The printed past form itatta is retained.

runs.text: Chegou o tempo, ouhora da propagação daley;

lines.note: Translates the example as the arrival of the time or hour for propagation of the law. Printed ouhora and daley remain joined; the statement continues with &c. below.
Toki wo uru means finding or obtaining a good opportunity. The Portuguese oca- continues into the following short line.
Completes ocasião, opportunity, together with tempo. The scan supports ſião after oca-, without the OCR’s extra t.

runs.text: ¶ Tem os Iapoẽs ſeis horasde dia, & ſeis

lines.note: A new paragraph explains the Japanese division into six daytime and six nighttime hours. The visible paragraph mark omitted by OCR is restored; horasde remains joined as printed.

runs.text: de noite, as quais contão por nomes de deze

lines.note: Continues the account of naming the hours after animals. The enumeration below contains twelve names; the locally printed vowel in deze is retained rather than silently regularized from that number.
Begins the twelve animal names: rat, ox, tiger, hare and dragon. They are Japanese terms embedded in the Portuguese explanation; the list continues on the next physical row.

runs.text: Mi, Vma, Fitçuji, Saru, Tori, Inu, Y.

lines.note: Completes the animal list with snake, horse, sheep, monkey, cock, dog and boar. Vma and Y are retained as the printed romanizations.

runs.text: Pollos quaes parece que entendem doze ſignos

lines.note: The compiler interprets these names as twelve celestial signs. This is the dictionary’s explanatory comparison, not a modern correction of the Japanese timekeeping system.
Celeſtes completes the sentence about celestial signs. OCR Ouz is not printed on this row; it arose from adjacent material and is removed.
Toki here functions as when. Tera ye mairoo toki gives the example of coming to the church; the initial capital T replaces OCR r.

runs.text: do vier à igreja, ou na hora em que vier.

lines.note: Completes the Portuguese temporal example: when one comes to church, or at the hour when one comes. It belongs to the preceding toki construction.
This toki is the meal of Buddhist monks. Toki and hiji are paired in the example and glossed below as the two meals.
Gives dinner and supper of the monks as the explanation of the paired Japanese meal terms. It is a short continuation of the preceding entry.
Toki, alternatively toki no koe, is the shout given when beginning battle. Latin l introduces the synonymous phrase.
Completes the battle-opening context and starts toki wo aguru, raising the battle cry, with another verb alternative to follow.
Tsukuru supplies the alternative verb for giving the battle cry before charging. The Portuguese Dargrita is printed closely joined.
The battle cry is compared with invoking Santiago. The comparison belongs to the Portuguese gloss, and Sanctiago retains its historical spelling.
Toki, toku, toita is glossed first as untying and then melting. The principal forms belong to this verb entry rather than the preceding noun toki.
Completes derreter, melting; dangui wo toku illustrates preaching or expounding a discourse. The Japanese verb therefore also has an explanatory sense.
Tokyaku denotes vomiting; tokyaku suru is the verbal example. The repeated Japanese form and the Portuguese infinitive vomiting agree; Vt belongs to the italic apparatus.

runs.text: Adu. De quando em quando, ou

lines.note: Tokidoki means from time to time, as the Portuguese adverbial definition states. The scan shows the capital T that OCR read as r.
Completes the alternative Portuguese expression de tempo em tempo. This continuation has the same intermittent meaning as the preceding row.
Tokihakari is another word for a clock. The capital T is restored from the scan; the gloss agrees with tokei earlier in the column.
Tokihanashi means releasing or untying. The principal part ita is retained as printed rather than expanded from an expected modern inflection.

runs.text: deixar ir como homem, ou animal que eſtaua

lines.note: The definition continues with letting a person or animal go. This gives the object and consequence of the release described above.
Completes the release definition by specifying that the person or animal had been captive. The row is ordinary body text at the bottom of the first column.

Tokihodoki means untangling or untying. Reinspection of the abraded round vowels and repeated fodoqu below supports Toqifodoqi rather than OCR Teqifodeqi; the weak vowel before the final qi remains a nonblocking graphic caveat. The supplied NINJAL Entry Words Data of Nippojisho (Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html) corroborates the headword after independent reading, but does not determine this impression’s spelling.
Kami wo toki hodoku means untangling the hair. The Portuguese starts the equivalent desempeçar across the row boundary, while the Japanese preserves its printed internal space.
Completes the gloss as disentangling the hairs of the head. This specifies the bodily meaning of kami in the preceding example.

runs.text: Pentẽ ralo pera pentear os cabelos.

lines.note: Tokigushi is a comb with widely spaced teeth for combing hair. Pentẽ retains the printed abbreviation mark, without supplying an unprinted final consonant.
Tokimeki describes the season or opportunity in which something flourishes. The printed principal forms u and eita are retained; the Portuguese division is conjun- followed by ção.

runs.text: ção em que florece algũa couſa, como tempo das

lines.note: Completes conjunção and gives the time of flowers as an example of flourishing. The OCR’s final l is the adjacent rule, not a letter after das.

runs.text: flores em que todos ſaem a ver, & recrearſe.

lines.note: Continues the flowering-season example: everyone goes out to look and enjoy themselves. The whole line belongs to the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Ser tempo em q̃ hum florece em ri-

lines.note: Introduces another use of tokimeki: a time when a person flourishes in wealth. A visible terminal mark divides ri- from quezas below.
Completes riquezas and adds bonança, prosperity or good fortune. The visible o corrects OCR banança; the final &c. closes the example.
Tokimeki ayeri describes people gathering in celebration during a period of a household’s prosperity. S. is the upright written-usage label, separate from the italic Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: gẽte de varias partes cõ aluoroço, & alegria a

lines.note: The people gather from various places with excitement and joy. Gẽte has a tilde, not a grave accent; the final a introduces the infinitives on the next row.

runs.text: folgar, ou auiſitarſe por ſer tempo em que os

lines.note: Continues with celebrating or visiting because the household is enjoying favorable times. The scan reads folgar, with a, rather than OCR folgor; auiſitarſe retains the printed joining.
The family members are flourishing in prosperity. This relative clause explains why visitors come, rather than beginning another meaning of the headword.
Wealth and favor complete the family’s advantages. Priuança is the historical spelling of the favor or privileged access mentioned by the gloss.

Tokimidashi is loosening something into disorder, such as disheveling hair. The damaged Japanese headword reads midaxi, not nuidaxi; Portuguese emburulhar is retained as visibly printed rather than normalized.
Kami wo toki mi- begins the example of loosening and disheveling hair. The divided Japanese word continues as daſu; OCR mri- inserts a letter not supported by the scan.
Daſu completes midasu. The Portuguese says to dishevel, untie and release, with ſol- continuing into tar below rather than OCR ſel-.
Completes soltar os cabellos, releasing the hair. This is the end of the preceding example, not part of the following timekeeper entry.

runs.text: O que tem cuidado das horas, ou

lines.note: Tokimori is the person responsible for the hours or the clock. The gloss identifies an attendant or keeper rather than the measuring instrument itself.
Relogio completes the alternative object of the keeper’s care. The short line remains a distinct physical continuation.

runs.text: Hum barretinho que poem nas cucuru-

lines.note: Tokin is a small cap worn on the crowns of the heads. The word cucuru- continues as tas on the next row.
The wearers are Yamabuxis, the mountain ascetics. The scan’s initial Y corrects OCR V; the Japanese designation occurs within the Portuguese explanation.
Toki ni yotte is glossed adverbially as sometimes. Preserve the printed joined Toqiniyotte rather than imposing modern word boundaries.
The alternative gloss de quando em quando reinforces the occasional meaning. It closes the preceding adverbial entry.
Tokinobe means loosening and extending or paying out something. The first part of the definition connects untying with the subsequent lengthening.

runs.text: do como corda, ou amarra alargar, ou arriar.

lines.note: A rope or mooring line is given as the object that can be lengthened or let out. The example below makes the nautical application explicit.

Tomozzuna wo toki noburu means releasing or letting out the ship’s mooring line. The mark after Largar is compact, low and rounded like a period in enlargement, not the OCR’s hyphen; its unusual position before the continuing object is preserved.
Completes the mooring-line translation, then begins dangui wo tokinoburu, extending or expounding a discourse. The Japanese verb continues onto the next row.
Buru completes tokinoburu. Prègar gives the preaching sense, preserving its printed grave accent.

runs.text: Grita que ſe dà no principio da

lines.note: Toki no koe is the shout raised at the beginning of battle. This separate entry repeats the phrase already explained in the first column.
Batalha completes the battle-cry definition. Although some middle letter ink is weak, the surviving strokes support the existing word.

runs.text: Couſa como fruita que ha em

lines.note: Toki no keibutsu is something seasonal, with fruit as the example. Couſa and ha em restore the Portuguese words where OCR supplied Caouſa and ba m.
The fruit or other seasonal thing occurs at particular times. This completes the seasonal definition rather than introducing an additional headword.
Tokinkei is paraphrased as a bird living on Tosaku mountain. The printed phrase Toſacu yamani ſumu tori is preserved, and No- begins the Portuguese nome on the following row.

runs.text: me de hum paßaro que anda em hum monte cha

lines.note: Completes nome and describes a bird inhabiting a named mountain. Cha continues into mado on the next row without a securely printed terminal hyphen.
Mado completes chamado and identifies the mountain as Toſacuyama. The name is embedded within the Portuguese definition and is retained in its printed typeface.
Tookyoo is explained as the eastern capital, higashi no miyako. The initial circumflex and final caron are distinct; the entry is not evidence by itself for identification with the modern city name.
Oriente completes the geographical explanation, the capital on the eastern side. It is a short continuation of the preceding entry.

runs.text: Comer que ſe dà por eſmola aos Bon

lines.note: Tokiryoo is food given as alms to traveling Buddhist monks. Bon begins Bonzos across the line break; the final n is not OCR r.
Completes Bonzos and the pilgrimage context, then begins the request tokiryoo tabe. The example has a circumflex in Toqiriô, unlike the headword’s caron, and that printed distinction is retained.

runs.text: Daime de comer: palaura que dizem os

lines.note: Be completes tabe, here used as a request to be given food. Daime de comer supplies the Portuguese translation and identifies it as an utterance used by the monks.
Bonzos completes the identification of the speakers. The short row is ordinary continuation text.
Toki toki means each hour and also the particular hour or time set for something. The second explanation continues below.

runs.text: tempo determinado pera algũa couſa. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the appointed-time definition and introduces an example. The abbreviation Vt is in the Portuguese italic apparatus.
Toki toki ni mono wo suru means doing something at the specified times or each hour. The Japanese phrase is followed by the start of its Portuguese translation.

runs.text: couſa em determinadas horas, ou em cada hora.

lines.note: Completes the translation: doing something at determined hours or in each hour. Both interpretations correspond to the two meanings introduced above.

runs.text: As vezes, ou de tempo ẽ tẽpo.

lines.note: Toki to shite means at times or from time to time. The visible capital T replaces OCR r, while the Portuguese nasal abbreviations remain unexpanded.
